name: EdgeX Foundry
vendor: LF Edge (Linux Foundation), started at Dell

foundation.via: A Linux Foundation project since April 2017; one of LF Edge’s five founding projects

summary: A set of microservices for an edge gateway that talk to devices in their own protocols, such as Modbus, BACnet or OPC UA, turn every reading into a common event, and pass it on to rules, local apps or the cloud.
intro: Factories and buildings are full of equipment that speaks old field protocols over serial lines and local networks, not MQTT to the cloud. EdgeX Foundry runs on a gateway or industrial PC next to that equipment. On the south side, device services act as connectors, one per protocol: the project maintains services for Modbus, BACnet, OPC UA, Siemens S7, SNMP, GPIO, USB cameras, MQTT, REST and more, with SDKs in Go and C for writing others. Each device is described by a device profile, a YAML or JSON file that lists its resources (a temperature, a switch, a register) with types and read/write rights, and the commands built from them. Core Metadata keeps the profiles and the list of devices, Core Command turns a REST call into a read or write on a real device, and Core Data can store what devices send.

Readings travel as events on the EdgeX message bus, which is MQTT by default since version 4.0. On the north side, application services subscribe to events, filter and transform them in a pipeline of functions and send them on to a cloud service, a database or an enterprise system; they are written with SDKs in Go or, since 4.0, Python, or configured without code. The docs list the eKuiper rules engine among the supporting services, next to a scheduler and notifications. All the pieces are separate services, normally run as Docker containers, and the recommended minimum is 1 GB of memory and 3 GB of disk; the community supports amd64 and arm64.

EdgeX 4.0 “Odesa”, released in March 2025, is the third long-term support release, supported until March 2027; patches 4.0.1 and 4.0.2 followed. It replaced components whose licences had moved away from Apache-2.0-compatible terms: PostgreSQL became the default database instead of Redis, OpenBao replaced HashiCorp Vault as the secret store, and the project’s own Core Keeper replaced Consul for configuration and service registry.
strengths: Connectors for many industrial and building protocols out of the box, so old equipment can feed modern systems without new firmware
Device profiles separate what a device offers from how it is wired, so apps read `Temperature` instead of a Modbus register address
Vendor-neutral, Apache 2.0 and an LF Edge Impact-stage project, with long-term support releases that last two years
Each service can be replaced or extended, and app services can send data to any cloud rather than one provider’s IoT platform
limits: Many moving parts for one gateway: a message bus, a database, a secret store, a registry and a dozen services to run, secure and upgrade
Only amd64 and arm64 are supported; small 32-bit Arm boards need self-built binaries, and the minimum is a 1 GB machine, not a microcontroller
Data is kept on the gateway itself, so retention needs disk: the docs recommend about 32 GB to start, depending on how long readings are kept
The LTS policy covers the core services and SDKs, but not the reference device services, the GUI or third-party components such as PostgreSQL and OpenBao

story: Industrial IoT in the mid-2010s was a patchwork: every gateway vendor and cloud platform had its own way of talking to sensors and machines, and integrators wrote the same protocol glue again for each project. Dell had built IoT gateway software of its own under the name FUSE, and offered it as the seed of a shared, vendor-neutral middle layer instead.

On April 24, 2017 the Linux Foundation launched EdgeX Foundry with Dell’s FUSE code, more than a dozen microservices and over 125,000 lines under Apache 2.0, and about 50 founding members, among them AMD, Canonical, Linaro and VMware. Releases are named after places in alphabetical order, and 1.0 was tagged in June 2019. In January 2019 EdgeX became one of the five founding projects of LF Edge, where it later reached the Impact stage.

Major versions followed in 2021 (2.0) and 2023 (3.0 “Minnesota”). For 4.0 “Odesa” in March 2025 it swapped out Redis, Vault and Consul after their licences changed, making PostgreSQL, OpenBao and its own Core Keeper the defaults.

choices.choice: Microservices instead of one gateway program
choices.why: Each protocol connector, data service and export service runs in its own process, so a vendor can replace one part, or write it in another language, without forking the rest.
Describing devices in YAML or JSON lets a new model of sensor be added by writing a file rather than code, and gives northbound apps the same names whatever the protocol.
When Redis, Vault and Consul moved to source-available licences, EdgeX replaced them in 4.0 so that the whole default stack stayed open source.
